message.content:
### Tenant Rights in Texas (as of 2024) | Area | Key Rights | How to Exercise Them | |------|------------|----------------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlord may charge up to **one month’s rent** for a furnished unit and **two months’ rent** for an unfurnished unit.
• Must be returned within **30 days** after lease ends, minus any lawful deductions. | • Keep a copy of the lease and any receipts for repairs.
• Request a written itemized statement of deductions. | | **Habitability** | • Landlord must keep the premises in a safe, sanitary condition (plumbing, heating, electrical, etc.).
• Must comply with all building, health, and safety codes. | • Report problems in writing (email or letter).
• If unresolved, you may file a complaint with the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA) or local code enforcement. | | **Rent Increases** | • No statutory limit on how much rent can increase, but it must be in writing and given **at least 30 days’ notice** for month‑to‑month leases. | • Review your lease for any rent‑increase clauses.
• Ask for a written notice if you’re unsure. | | **Lease Termination** | • Either party may terminate a month‑to‑month lease with **30 days’ written notice**.
• For fixed‑term leases, you can break the lease only if the landlord breaches the lease or if you have a “just cause” (e.g., landlord fails to maintain habitability). | • Provide written notice and keep a copy.
• If breaking early, negotiate a settlement or seek legal advice. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • Landlord cannot enter without **reasonable notice** (usually 24 hours) unless it’s an emergency. | • Keep a log of any unannounced entries. | | **Discrimination** | • Landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income (including public assistance). | • File a complaint with the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) or TDHCA if you suspect discrimination. | | **Repair and Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to repair a major issue, you may repair it yourself and deduct the cost from rent, but you must follow proper procedures (written notice, receipts, etc.). | • Document the problem, send written notice, keep receipts, and give the landlord a chance to fix it before deducting. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlord must provide a **written notice** (usually 3 days for nonpayment, 30 days for lease violations).
• Eviction must go through court; landlords cannot forcibly remove tenants. | • Respond promptly to notices.
• Seek legal counsel if you receive an eviction notice. | | **Privacy** | • Landlord must respect your privacy; they can’t conduct searches without a warrant or court order unless you consent. | • Keep records of any unauthorized entries. | | **Utilities** | • Landlord can require you to pay utilities unless otherwise specified in the lease. | • Verify utility responsibilities in the lease. | | **Subletting & Assignment** | • Many leases allow subletting or assignment with landlord’s written consent. | • Obtain written permission before subletting. | | **Landlord’s Right to Enter** | • Landlord may enter for inspections, repairs, or to show the unit to prospective tenants, but must give **reasonable notice** (usually 24 hours). | • Keep a log of entries and verify notice was given. | #### Practical Steps to Protect Your Rights 1. **Read Your Lease Carefully** – Understand all terms, especially those about rent, deposits, maintenance, and termination. 2. **Keep Written Records** – Emails, texts, and written notices are your best evidence if disputes arise. 3. **Know the Law** – Familiarize yourself with the Texas Property Code (especially Chapters 92–95) and local ordinances. 4. **Use Official Channels** – File complaints with TDHCA, HUD, or local code enforcement when necessary. 5. **Seek Legal Advice** – If you face eviction, discrimination, or significant disputes, consult a tenant‑rights attorney or a nonprofit legal aid organization. --- **Disclaimer:** This information is general and not legal advice. Laws can change, and local ordinances may add additional protections. For specific situations, consult a qualified attorney or a local tenant‑rights organization.
